draft.title: Protection and assimilation
card: state and territory laws from the late 1800s that placed First Nations Australians under government control. Officials often decided where people lived, worked and married, and how their wages were spent.
a policy from the 1930s that expected First Nations Australians to give up their cultures and live like white Australians.
Both policies were made by governments without the agreement of First Nations people. Both took away choices that other Australians had.
The two differ in aim. Protection controlled people, often on reserves and missions. Assimilation aimed to make their cultures disappear into the wider community.
draft.remember: Protection controlled where and how people lived. Assimilation expected them to give up their cultures.

a.q: Which best describes assimilation policy from the 1930s?
opts: It expected First Nations people to give up their cultures
It let First Nations people choose where to live and work
It aimed to keep First Nations cultures apart from others
It gave First Nations communities control of their affairs
a.why: Assimilation expected First Nations people to give up their cultures and live like white Australians. The option about keeping cultures apart is tempting, but it describes the opposite aim, since assimilation wanted cultures to disappear.
a.clue: Think about what people were expected to give up.

b.q: In the 1940s, an official in Western Australia tells a young Aboriginal woman to move to a town, take a job in a white household and stop speaking her language. Which aim does this show?
opts: Assimilation, as she is told to live like white Australians
Protection, as an official is deciding things for her
Equal rights, as she is free to choose her own job
Self-rule, as First Nations people run their own affairs
b.why: She is told to take up a white way of life and drop her language, which is the aim of assimilation. Protection is tempting because an official controls her life, but the card says protection policies controlled people, often on reserves and missions, and did not set out to end their cultures.
b.clue: Look at what she is told to stop doing.

a.best: It expected First Nations people to give up their cultures

b.best: Assimilation, as she is told to live like white Australians
also_right: Protection, as an official is deciding things for her

problems.detail: The scenario has an official deciding where she lives and works, which is exactly how the card defines protection. In 1940s WA these women were also still under protection law (Native Administration Act 1936). So the protection option can be defended. The scenario should rely on the cultural element alone, or the stem should ask more plainly about the policy's aim of ending culture.

The why says 'the card says' protection 'did not set out to end their cultures', but the card never says this. It is also historically doubtful: under protection, officials such as A.O. Neville in WA pursued the absorption of Aboriginal people of mixed descent.
The clue 'Think about what people were expected to give up' repeats the wording of the right option ('expected ... to give up'), so it hands students the answer without testing the idea.

proposal.title: Protection and assimilation
card: state and territory laws from the late 1800s that placed First Nations Australians under government control. Officials often decided where people lived, worked and married, and how their wages were spent.
a policy from the 1930s that expected First Nations Australians to give up their cultures and live like white Australians.
Both policies were made by governments without the agreement of First Nations people. Both took away choices that other Australians had.
The focus differed. Protection was mainly about controlling people, often on reserves and missions. Assimilation made ending their cultures the openly stated goal.
proposal.remember: Protection centred on control of people's lives. Assimilation openly aimed to replace their cultures with a white way of life.

a.q: Which best describes assimilation policy from the 1930s?
opts: It expected First Nations people to give up their cultures
It let First Nations people choose where to live and work
It aimed to keep First Nations cultures apart from others
It gave First Nations communities control of their affairs
a.why: Assimilation expected First Nations people to give up their cultures and live like white Australians. Keeping cultures apart is tempting, but assimilation aimed for the opposite: it wanted First Nations cultures to disappear into the wider community.
a.clue: To assimilate means to be absorbed into something else.

b.q: In the 1950s, a government leaflet urges First Nations families to stop speaking their languages and drop their customs. Which policy aim does it show?
opts: Assimilation, as it asks families to drop their cultures
Protection, as officials control where families live
Equal rights, as families keep their own languages
Self-rule, as communities run their own affairs
b.why: The leaflet asks families to give up their languages and customs, which is the openly stated goal of assimilation. Protection is tempting because both policies were made by government, but nothing in the leaflet controls where families live, work or marry.
b.clue: Ask what the leaflet wants families to stop doing.
